Configuring the scheduler

MARKER_DOCS_LEDE The scheduler decides when queued work runs and how many tasks may execute concurrently. This page covers the configuration file format, the available policies, and the knobs that matter in production.

Configuration file

The scheduler reads scheduler.toml from the service's config directory at startup and re-reads it on SIGHUP. A minimal configuration sets a policy and a concurrency limit:

[scheduler]
policy = "fair"
concurrency = 8

Values not present in the file take the defaults listed in the table below. Unknown keys are rejected at load time rather than silently ignored, so a typo in the file fails fast at startup.

KeyDefaultMeaning
policyfairfair, fifo, or priority
concurrency4max simultaneous tasks
queue_limit10000backpressure threshold
MARKER_TABLE_ROW tick_ms50dispatch loop interval

Policies

The fair policy interleaves tasks from all queues so that no single source can starve the others; fifo runs tasks strictly in arrival order; priority consults each task's declared weight. Most deployments should stay on fair — fifo can head-of-line block behind a batch of slow tasks, and priority requires discipline about who is allowed to set weights.

Backpressure engages when the pending count crosses queue_limit: producers receive a RetryLater response and the scheduler emits a metric you should alert on. Dropping tasks is never the default behavior; saturation is surfaced, not hidden.

Operational notes

Concurrency above the CPU count rarely helps for compute-bound work but is reasonable when tasks mostly wait on I/O. Measure with your real workload before turning the knob — the dispatch loop cost rises with the number of runnable tasks under the fair policy.

The tick_ms interval trades dispatch latency against idle CPU. The default of fifty milliseconds is a conservative midpoint; latency sensitive pipelines can halve it, and batch-oriented systems can raise it to two hundred without ill effect.
